h: After the vote and the courts, the street is the last right left
dek: Aakar Patel argues that when both the voter list and the courts lose trust, taking to the street is the real test of democracy that remains.
body: Aakar Patel counts three tools of democracy: the vote, the courts and protest. He argues that only the third is fully in the citizen's own hands. We think of the vote as another name for democracy, but according to the writer, the days when Indian elections had full credibility are now behind us.

The Constitution gives every adult the right to be a voter, a right that can be taken away only on a few narrow grounds. Patel charges that the Election Commission is treating this right like a piece of advice. In the last four weeks he has counted about a dozen U-turns: a new drive to add back names that were cut, a softer rule on the declaration form, a review of faulty software, and on third-party objections, mostly against Muslim voters, only a limit and not a ban.

According to the writer, this rush of fixes itself shows that the whole exercise began carelessly and is now being wound up in panic. The damage still will not be undone, because citizens are now split into many boxes: voters, those whose names were cut, those who have appealed, and those who do not even know where they stand. Even a full rollback after an election raises a question of legitimacy, and he sees an example of this in West Bengal.

Article 32 gives the right to go to court, but not a guarantee of a good verdict. According to Patel, the courts too have grown weaker. A government can influence the vote and the courts, but it is hard to control the bodies of people who come out on the street. That is why governments crush protest more than anything else.

He gives two examples: the farmers who sat at Delhi's borders got three laws withdrawn, and the movement of Muslim women stopped an Assam-style NRC from spreading to the rest of the country. In the writer's view, the SIR is still on that same path, and the young people who have come out on Delhi's streets are the most hopeful news of this time.
nazar: The heaviest point in Patel's list is that the objections were filed mostly against Muslim voters. When a name being cut from the voter list becomes the first step towards doubting citizenship, it is migrant workers, poor women, and Dalit and Adivasi (indigenous) settlements that get caught first in the web of paperwork.

A dozen U-turns are not proof of the Commission's honesty; they are the result of pressure from the street. That is the lesson of this article: rights on paper survive only when people stand up for them.
sawal: If the vote and the courts grow tired, what does democracy rely on?
ref: Article 32
The provision of the Constitution that gives a citizen the right to go straight to the Supreme Court for fundamental rights. Ambedkar called it the soul of the Constitution.
SIR
The Special Intensive Revision of the voter list. Voters are asked for documents and the list is made afresh, and there are charges that names were cut on a large scale.
ank: Roughly the number of U-turns by the Commission in four weeks
Tools of democracy: the vote, the courts and protest

h: A spark is not enough: the Cockroach movement needs organisation
dek: Ashok Swain says that after its July win, the Cockroach Janta Party fell behind in October because it had a crowd but no structure.
body: Ashok Swain, a professor at Uppsala University, is a sympathiser of the Cockroach Janta Party, but here he takes stock. In July, anger over paper leaks and unemployment turned this platform, which began as satire, into a nationwide movement, and Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan had to go. In October the party came out demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. The charge is that more than 13 crore names were cut from voter lists, with minorities, Dalits and the poor making up a larger share; the Commission and the BJP deny this.

According to the writer, the first weakness lay in the issue itself. Paper leaks hit students directly. In the fight over the voter list, the real claimants are the political parties, which have evidence, lawyers, Parliament and organisation. Rahul Gandhi was already raising this question, so the direction of the campaign did not stay in the Cockroach party's hands.

The second weakness was that the advantage of surprise was gone. In July the government had taken it for an internet joke; in October it was ready and waiting. On 10 October Abhijeet Dipke, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka were stopped at the airport itself, and at least 7,000 people were detained. According to Swain, the government looked rattled but won on tactics.

The third gap is organisation. The movement rested on a few faces, online calls and Jantar Mantar, so when the leaders were removed, no network sprang into action on its own. The writer explains the difference between a committee and an organisation: district units, local workers, safe communication and a second line of leaders. Meanwhile AISA, AISF and SFI leaned towards the larger opposition front, and Neha Bora was seen marching with Rahul and Priyanka Gandhi.

Swain's advice is that the party should join the opposition campaign while keeping its identity, and later become an independent pressure group on education, jobs, health and affordable housing, one that does not trail behind any party.
nazar: This criticism comes from a friend, not an enemy, and that is why it is valuable. Of the crores of names said to have been cut from the voter list, the largest share is said to belong to those whose voices are already heard less: Muslims, Dalits, Adivasis, migrant workers and poor women. For them this fight is not a trend but something as basic as citizenship, and trends are short-lived.

In our view the real lesson is that the parliament of the street will last only if it reaches the neighbourhoods, small towns and settlements where names have been cut. Jantar Mantar can be shut; not every lane can.
sawal: Can a movement carry on after its leaders are arrested?
ref: Cockroach Janta Party
A youth platform that began as satire on social media in May 2026. Its founder is Abhijeet Dipke; after its movement against paper leaks in July, the Education Minister resigned.
SIR
Special Intensive Revision, that is, a special intensive revision of voter lists. The opposition charges that in its name the names of genuine voters were cut on a large scale.
photo_note: Snowstorm: Hannibal's army crossing the Alps

h: 'Regime change' is not an insult, it is democracy's medicine
dek: A Deshbandhu editorial says that calling a demand for a change of government sedition is really a way to dodge questions about vote theft.
body: The Deshbandhu editorial begins with the phrase that has made the government uneasy: regime change. The paper's argument is simple. In a democracy, changing who holds power, raising the slogan 'vote thief' or demanding a resignation is not a crime but the very foundation of the system. Changing power is wrong only when it involves violence, illegal acts or unethical means.

According to the editorial, Rajnath Singh cornered the opposition on this very issue, the same note was heard in Mohan Bhagwat's Vijayadashami speech, and Kiren Rijiju cited Bangladesh and France to call India's protest wrong. The paper describes violent movements in several European countries and says that where there is arson and attack, calling it a 'riot' makes sense, but India's picture is the opposite.

In October Delhi Police used force on peaceful protesters, while the movement did not give up non-violence and patience. The editorial remarks wryly that if Gandhi raised his voice against vote theft today, he too would get jail or the baton. The paper's demands are clear: remove Gyanesh Kumar, give answers on the SIR, bring back the old selection committee of the Prime Minister, the Leader of the Opposition and the Chief Justice, and end the lifelong legal protection given to the Chief Election Commissioner.

The editorial asks why Home Minister Amit Shah did not answer in Parliament on the violence at Jantar Mantar in July. At the end it recalls Gandhi's testimony before the Hunter Committee in 1920, where he said that even in a free country, satyagraha against an unjust law can be a citizen's duty. The paper concludes that what is a sin for the BJP is a cure and a hope for democracy.
nazar: The game of calling every disagreement a foreign plot or 'regime change' is not new, but this time its target is questions tied directly to the right to vote. Among those whose names were cut, a large number are the poor, migrant workers and minorities, and calling their complaint sedition is to push them out a second time.
sawal: Since when is demanding a change of government against democracy?
ref: Hunter Committee
A committee set up by the British government to inquire into the 1919 Jallianwala Bagh massacre. Gandhi gave testimony before it.
photo_note: The Passing of Shah Jahan, Abanindranath Tagore

h: A worn-out script: infiltrator, foreign hand and urban Naxal
dek: Sagarika Ghose argues that the government's old weapons for smearing protesters are not working this time.
body: In this article, Trinamool Congress Rajya Sabha MP and journalist Sagarika Ghose takes apart, one by one, the script the government has used to smear every movement. She says the Cockroach Janta Party and Gen Z youth are on the street even though some of their leaders are in custody, the opposition is with them, and the demand is clear: Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar must go and a new Election Commission must be formed.

The first weapon is the infiltrator. The government calls the SIR a clean-up of infiltrators. According to the writer, 13.39 crore names were removed from the draft lists in three phases, and these include deaths, changes of address and duplicate names. The question is how many of them actually turned out to be foreigners. She says RTI requests and questions in Parliament got no answer. In Bengal, 93 per cent of those whose appeals were heard got their names back, which means cutting them was wrong in the first place, yet lakhs of appeals are still pending.

The second weapon is foreign funding, for which no evidence has been put forward. Ghose calls it a new form of the 'foreign hand' line from Indira Gandhi's time. The third charge is anarchy, while according to her the real disorder came from cancelling the Jantar Mantar notification, putting up barricades, shutting metro stations and attacks by Hindutva gangs.

The fourth label is 'urban Naxal', which the writer says was coined to make dissent look frightening. On the street are students, professors, doctors, artists and parents, and the issues have now spread to jobs, education and civil liberties. Her answer to the noise about regime change is simple: changing the government through elections is exactly the opposition's job.

The article ends with four questions: how many names were cut and why, how many of them were proven to be foreigners, what protection is there for names cut wrongly, and where is the evidence of foreign money.
nazar: It is worth keeping in mind that the writer is herself an opposition MP, but her questions belong not to any party but to every voter. The infiltrator label sticks first to Muslims, Matuas and migrant workers in Bengal and Assam, who have to make rounds of offices to show papers.
If 93 per cent of those who appealed were proven right, what about those who could not even reach an appeal? The right to vote should not depend on who has a lawyer and time.
sawal: Of the crores of names cut, how many actually turned out to be foreigners?
ref: Urban Naxal
A phrase coined by BJP leaders, used to link unarmed intellectuals and activists with Naxalism (Maoist armed insurgency).
Jantar Mantar notification
Jantar Mantar in Delhi was long the fixed place for sit-ins and protests. In October 2026, during this movement, it was removed from the list of protest sites.

h: A government of fear: battalions instead of talks
dek: According to Anant K. Sahay, the government's response to the anti-SIR movement shows it wants to suppress the people, not talk to them.
body: Anant K. Sahay, who writes on politics and foreign affairs, believes the protest that began against the SIR has now become a large movement in which young people and opposition parties stand together. According to him, about 13 crore people lost their right to vote in this process, and that is why the demand to remove Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar is so strong.

The writer's central argument is that the government is responding with fear and repression instead of dialogue. He notes that at the height of the movement, about 40 battalions, or roughly 40 thousand personnel, were deployed in a small area of New Delhi, while even in the worst phase of militancy in Kashmir the deployment was about 100 battalions. Dozens of metro stations were shut, about 250 trains were cancelled, and protesters, journalists and even women were beaten. He also repeats the charges that weapons were pointed at a peaceful crowd in Bihar and that pellet guns were fired at Jantar Mantar in July, though he himself offers the idea of a Home Ministry order behind these only as a guess.

Sahay sees a political calculation behind this harshness. According to him, the BJP, reduced to 240 seats in 2024 and dependent on allies, is busy bending the electoral system itself in its favour: the SIR, the changed method of appointing election commissioners, and lifelong legal protection for the commissioners. He also puts the Supreme Court in the dock for not recognising these dangers.

The writer's sarcasm on the propaganda war is sharp. On one side the Prime Minister calls India the mother of democracy on the world stage; on the other, the place for sit-ins in the capital is shut down. The pro-government media's noise about regime change reminds him of Orwell's novel 1984. His conclusion is that the movement's goal is to get the SIR withdrawn.
nazar: Sahay's tone is bitter and the source of many of his figures is not given in the article, so they should be read only as the writer's claims. Still, the comparison with Kashmir is worth pausing on: when the capital's citizens are handled the way an uprising is, the treatment that border regions, Adivasi forests and Muslim settlements have faced for decades has now reached the middle of the city.
The biggest price of shut metros and cancelled trains is paid by daily wage workers, women domestic workers and small shopkeepers, whether or not they have anything to do with the movement.
sawal: A Kashmir-like deployment in the capital, to deal with whom?
ref: Battalion
A unit of the Central Armed Police Forces, usually made up of about a thousand personnel.
Election Commissioners Appointment Act, 2023
This law removed the Chief Justice of India from the selection committee and put in a Union minister chosen by the Prime Minister, which raised questions about the Commission's independence.

h: Cockroaches under siege, parties on edge: why both BJP and Congress are wary
dek: According to Aditya Menon, the crackdown on the Cockroach Janta Party has brought four leaders from outside the INDIA alliance to its side.
body: In his newsletter, The Quint's political editor Aditya Menon points to an interesting contradiction. The government stopped the Cockroach Janta Party's Jantar Mantar 2.0, its spokespersons Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka were sent to judicial custody, and Jantar Mantar was removed from the list of protest sites altogether. On the surface the party looks besieged, but according to the writer, in this same period it has found support from unexpected corners.

Menon names four leaders who are not part of the INDIA alliance, yet all of them demanded the release of Das and Ranka. Former Andhra chief minister Jaganmohan Reddy, once seen as an informal ally of the BJP, has now expressed regret for supporting the 2023 law on appointing election commissioners. Odisha's Naveen Patnaik has drifted away from the BJP since his 2024 defeat. BRS's K.T. Rama Rao is openly anti-BJP. And the most unusual name is former Tamil Nadu BJP president K. Annamalai, who is building his own separate platform.

The writer argues that the ground of opposition to the BJP is widening and the Cockroach party is acting as a catalyst. This is bad news for the BJP, but not entirely good news for the Congress either. Many players such as AAP, DMK, BSP and Prashant Kishor are against the BJP but do not want to come under the Congress banner, and if the alliance breaks in the Uttar Pradesh election, the SP too may join this line.
According to Menon, what lies ahead will be decided by two things: how the Congress takes forward its campaign against Gyanesh Kumar, and how the Cockroach party reshapes its strategy.
nazar: This new line of opponents raises both hope and questions. Leaders who until yesterday kept silent on, or backed, the SIR or the laws on the Commission are now speaking up for young people in jail, and that is welcome. But the test will come when the question of names of the poor, Dalits and Muslims being cut arises in their own states.

In our view the real danger is that the question of the right to vote gets shrunk in the tug of war between parties. Before deciding who gains from the movement, it should be settled when the cut names will return.
sawal: Will Annamalai and Jagan's support strengthen the movement or blur it?
ref: Jantar Mantar 2.0
The Cockroach Janta Party's October call to gather again at Jantar Mantar, which police stopped by detaining leaders and sealing off the area.
INDIA alliance
An alliance of opposition parties formed in 2023, including the Congress, SP, Trinamool, DMK, the Left parties and several others.
photo_note: Representative image: an instrument at Jantar Mantar

h: A distant protest is easy to ignore: dissent evicted from Jantar Mantar
dek: A.J. Philip reminds us that the place of a protest is part of its message, and pushing it away from power is a ploy to make it toothless.
body: A.J. Philip begins with the Kerala of his childhood. Outside the taluk office in Pathanamthitta, an old naturopath would set up his small tent every day and sit in protest. His demand was impractical, yet no one questioned his right to sit there, and his protest ended only with his death.

Then the writer gives examples from London's Hyde Park, Washington, Berlin and Paris, where places of protest are often right in front of the buildings being protested against. Lafayette Square in front of the White House is one example.

In Delhi this place used to be the Boat Club near India Gate. In 1988 farmers led by Mahendra Singh Tikait camped there and the capital came to a halt. After that, Jantar Mantar was made the official place for protest. For more than thirty years this arrangement worked for both sides: protesters stayed close to Parliament and the ministries, and the police found it easier to manage crowds.

Now the government has removed Jantar Mantar from this list and suggested Ramlila Maidan, Burari and the CBD Ground as alternatives, which are far from the centre of power. Philip's argument is that even if ten lakh people gather at a distant place, the rulers will feel no inconvenience. A protest is not a fair but a demand for accountability, so its place is part of its message.

The writer sees an irony in this: an arrangement the government itself created is being broken just when people's anger turned out bigger than expected. The right to protest belongs not only to sensible demands or big crowds, but also to that lone man in his tent.
nazar: Jantar Mantar was where people came who got no hearing anywhere else: contract workers, displaced Adivasis, families who suffered caste atrocities against Dalits, young people asking for jobs. Sending protest to the edge of the city muffles their voices most of all, because they have no TV studio or lobby, only the street.
sawal: What kind of protest is one that power never even sees?
ref: Boat Club
The ground near India Gate that was once the main site of big protests in Delhi. After the 1988 farmers' sit-in, protests were sent to Jantar Mantar.
photo_note: Representative image: the Jantar Mantar observatory

h: Tricolour in hand, still detained: who holds the licence on patriotism?
dek: Iftikhar Ahmad Qadri asks: if even a peaceful march carrying the tricolour is under suspicion, where is the room left for dissent?
body: In this Urdu article, senior journalist Iftikhar Ahmad Qadri puts the events of 16 October at the centre. The Cockroach Janta Party and student groups had announced a 'Lehra Do Tiranga' (Wave the Tricolour) march in Connaught Place's Central Park, but before it could begin, Delhi Police detained several people including Abhijeet Dipke and AISA president Neha Bora and broke up the gathering.

The writer also lays out the background: charges of names being cut from the voter list on a large scale, the demand for Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar's resignation, the removal of Jantar Mantar from the list of protest sites, and Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das being sent to Tihar. He believes the charges should be investigated, because the statements of the Commission and the government differ.

Qadri's first argument is that waving the tricolour is not a crime in itself. A restriction on the place is a separate legal question, and even that is fair only when it is lawful, reasonable and proportionate. Stopping a march only because it criticises the government is dangerous for civil liberty. He asks the police to state the legal basis for the detentions and the government to give the reason for the Jantar Mantar decision.

His second argument is about who owns the flag. According to the writer, the tricolour is the symbol of a freedom struggle in which people of every religion, language and region took part, so no single camp has the right to hand out certificates of patriotism. A person who criticises the government is just as much a citizen.

In the end he argues for dialogue with young people: one may disagree with their demands, but silencing them before even listening is no solution. The flag is honoured only when every citizen under its shade feels equality and justice.
nazar: A Muslim writer reminding readers in Urdu that the tricolour belongs to all is itself a comment on these times. For communities asked every day for proof of loyalty, the sharpest question is who will define patriotism.

Arriving to detain people even before the flag was raised shows that the fear was not of the march's violence but of its picture: young people, the tricolour and the question of the vote, all together.
sawal: Who, after all, has the right to hand out certificates of patriotism?
ref: AISA
All India Students' Association, a student body linked to the CPI (ML) Liberation. Its president Neha Bora is a well-known face of this movement.

h: A new generation on Europe's streets: a revolt against cuts
dek: Anger that rose from France's crumbling schools has spread to Spain, Italy, Albania and Belgium, and Luca Tavan traces its root to the austerity policies after 2008.
body: In Red Flag, an Australian socialist paper, Luca Tavan says Europe is going through its biggest uprising of young people and workers in at least a generation. It began in late September in Créteil, a working-class suburb of Paris, where students blockaded their run-down school. On 17 October workers came out too, and about eight lakh people across the country joined strikes, marches and blockades.

The fire is not in France alone. In Spain, the eviction of an 87-year-old woman, whose rent rose 230 per cent after an investment company bought her flat, sparked a housing movement, and unions have called a general strike on 11 November. In Albania, opposition to a luxury resort linked to the Trump family grew into a national uprising together with demands on education and wages. In Milan, most of the 250 people detained were minors.

The writer finds one root for all of this: wage cuts after the 2008 crisis, youth unemployment and the knife taken to social services. Citing figures from Italy's Parliamentary Budget Office, he says real private-sector wages there have fallen 6.6 per cent since 1990, new jobs are insecure and rents are running ahead of pay.

The article's sharpest argument is about the link between weapons and cuts. France is cutting 54 billion euros from social spending and wants to double military spending. Macron complains about violence, but according to Tavan most of the clashes were sparked by police repression, in which one student lost a hand and another an eye.

The Indignados movement of 2011 kept unions and Left parties away from its marches, while today Madrid's protesters are openly embracing the workers' tradition. Despite the defeats of Podemos and Syriza, a new generation is looking for basic solutions. For the writer, the real question is how this anger can become organised strength.
nazar: This revolt in Europe is a reminder that when governments buy weapons at the cost of schools and hospitals, young people are the first to lose patience. In India too, the merging and closing of government schools, insecure jobs and rising rents weigh heaviest on families from Dalit, Adivasi, Muslim and working-class backgrounds.

The only difference is that here such anger is often dismissed as sedition or rioting. The world is watching police excess against minors in France; we should also listen to the silence on our own campuses and in our own settlements.
sawal: When will the leaking roofs of our government schools find a voice?
ref: Indignados
A youth movement against unemployment and cuts that rose in Spain in 2011, also called 15-M. The Podemos party later grew out of it.
Syriza
A Greek Left party that came to power in 2015 promising to oppose austerity. But under pressure from European creditors it had to impose those same cuts.

h: Selective anger over executions: the real question is the state's right
dek: Dilip Khan takes the outcry over the execution of two Bangladeshis in Mecca to the whole structure of the death penalty.
body: When Saudi Arabia executed Nazrul Islam and Siti Akhtar of Bangladesh in Mecca, anger poured out on social media. Dilip Khan says on his Substack that much of this anger was not against the death penalty but against a big punishment for a small crime. When the viral claim about a kiss on the forehead turned out to be baseless, the debate settled on whether anyone should be killed for sex.

The writer argues that this argument about proportion quietly accepts that the state may take a life for some crimes, and so it makes the death penalty firmer. The view against the death penalty, by contrast, says that no crime gives the state the right to take a life, that this punishment does not stop crime, and that it rarely reaches the powerful.

He reminds us that this is not about Saudi Arabia alone. Singapore hanged Tangaraju Suppiah in 2023 in a case involving about one kilo of cannabis, Indonesia executed two Australians in 2015, and India's NDPS law also provides for the death penalty. According to the writer, even the 'rarest of rare' test is not applied the same way in our country.

In his view, dismissing such punishments as medieval is the same Orientalism that Edward Said spoke of. Mohammed bin Salman, whom the West kept calling a reformer, set a record for executions during his own rule. According to the writer, Saudi Arabia executed at least 356 people in 2025, mostly in drug cases and mostly migrant workers from poor countries.

In the end he returns to India, where Ravji Rao and Surja Ram were hanged on the basis of a judgment that the Supreme Court later held to be wrong. The writer concludes that consistent opposition should not be against any religion or culture, but against this power of the state.
nazar: Lakhs of Indian workers work in the Gulf countries, and defending them in the courts there is often on no one's agenda. Anger wakes up only when a story goes viral, and in most cases not even then.

In India too, a large share of those sentenced to death come from poor, backward and minority communities, as the 2016 Death Penalty Report of National Law University Delhi has already shown. A society that weeps selectively over others' executions must question its own executions just as strictly.
sawal: Whose execution hurts us, and whose does not?
ref: Rarest of rare
In the 1980 Bachan Singh case, the Supreme Court said the death penalty should be given only in the rarest of rare cases. But this test has been read differently from court to court.
NDPS law
The 1985 law on narcotic drugs. Its Section 31A provides for the death penalty for repeat offences involving large quantities.

h: Be a good OCI: the demand for loyalty from Indians abroad
dek: The Modi government embraces Indians abroad for money and support, but strips the OCI status of those who ask questions.
body: New York-based human rights lawyer Devyani Kakkar writes in Scroll that after 2014, Prime Minister Modi worked hard to woo the roughly fifty lakh people of Indian origin in America for money, skills and political support. Memories of home and pride were woven into a shared identity, and getting Overseas Citizenship of India, or OCI, status was made easier.

But there is another side to this picture. Citing a 2024 Human Rights Watch report, the writer says more than a hundred OCIs were cancelled in a decade, and some people were expelled from the country on charges of disaffection towards the Constitution. This October, Imran Khan, an American citizen and OCI holder, got a notice to leave India after joining a peaceful protest in Mumbai, which he has challenged in the Bombay High Court.

This is not the only case. The article mentions journalist Aatish Taseer and academics Ashok Swain and Nitasha Kaul. The Delhi High Court overturned the decision to cancel Swain's OCI in March 2025, while Kaul said in May 2025 that her card had been cancelled and called it transnational repression.

The article's real question is about belonging. A bond made of food, language, clothing and politics does not break when one changes citizenship, yet some OCIs are embraced and others are thrown out despite those same bonds. According to the writer, in the West a good immigrant is one who blends in, and in India a good OCI is one who does not question the government.

So people abroad are caught between two countries that see them as skills or money rather than as whole human beings. The writer concludes that belonging cannot rest on the condition of agreeing with the government, and in a country born out of movements, joining a protest should not be a reason for being thrown out.
nazar: This sorting of good and bad Indians is not limited to those abroad. Inside the country too, Muslims, Dalit and Adivasi activists and students are asked again and again for proof of loyalty, and dissent is labelled anti-national.

When the status of scholars and journalists settled abroad is taken away because of their opinions, the message is for everyone else: keep quiet. Such silence is not a democracy's strength but its weakness.
sawal: Does belonging come only on the condition of agreeing with the government?
ref: OCI
Overseas Citizenship of India: a status given to people of Indian origin who have taken another country's citizenship. It allows them to come and go without a visa, live and work, but not to vote.

h: Punished for asking: the culture of obedience in Pakistan
dek: Quraish Khattak argues that Pakistan's real lack is not intelligence but a culture that rewards obeying orders instead of curiosity.
body: In The Friday Times, Quraish Khattak begins with the joint sitting of Parliament on 15 October, which put its seal on an emergency and governor's rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. According to him, arguments there were weighed not on evidence but on political loyalty. Whether a question is fair is decided by who is asking and who is being targeted.

The writer sees this as part of a larger pattern. At home, respect for elders often turns into bowing without question, and obedience becomes the measure of a good upbringing. In offices, juniors shy away from disagreeing with their bosses, and quietly saying yes is mistaken for teamwork.

Education figures deepen this picture. According to the Economic Survey 2025-26, literacy is 63 per cent, which means 37 out of every hundred people cannot read and write. Citing a government policy document, the writer says only five per cent of children get a decent standard of schooling and only 12 per cent reach higher education. A system built on rote learning and fixed answers hands out degrees, not the skill of thinking.

Social media has made things harder. There is more information but less ability to test it, so inflammatory lies spread easily. According to the writer, when religious interpretations and political convenience fix the results in advance, the search in science and history stops right there. From farming to governance, a society that punishes experiment cannot learn from its failures.

As a cure, he speaks of learning through understanding and projects instead of rote in schools, testing reasoning rather than memory, and welcoming questions at home and at work. In his view, the test of a progressive society is not the number of slogans but how fearlessly people can question beliefs.
nazar: On this side of the border this picture is not unfamiliar. Here too, rote learning, classrooms shaped by hierarchy and the habit of calling a questioning student anti-national have grown. The highest price is paid by those whose questions touch the settled order of caste, religion or gender: Dalit and Adivasi students, and women told to stay quiet at home.
Those in power find obedient citizens convenient, but no democracy stays alive without questions.
sawal: Do our schools teach children to ask questions or to stay quiet?
ref: Governor's rule
Under Pakistan's Constitution, rule by the centre through the governor in place of a province's elected government, after imposing an emergency. It is similar to President's Rule in India.

h: Liberia again: the long shadow of slavery over American deportations
dek: Two researchers argue that the Trump administration's deals to send migrants to third countries repeat the same racial thinking that created Liberia.
body: In 1816 white Americans formed the American Colonization Society to settle free Black people in Africa, because slave owners and even some opponents of slavery saw them as a threat. Liberia was born out of this project. Writing in Africa Is a Country, Natália Cintra and Tosin Durodola argue that America's deportation system today is reviving that same colonial model.

According to the writers, the second Trump administration has made return agreements, often secret, with at least 35 countries, mostly in the Global South, in which migrants are bargaining chips. On 18 August Liberia announced it would take up to 1,200 people from third countries. Two days later about 20 people arrived and 14 stayed, from Cameroon, Eritrea, Venezuela, Honduras, Colombia, Brazil and Guatemala. Several of them were people whom American courts had protected from return because of the risk of persecution.

There is also a story of pressure behind the deal. According to the writers, an American government document had placed Liberia among countries facing a possible travel ban and described taking in deportees as a way out, while American aid has fallen and the new health agreement is about 63 per cent smaller than before. The government calls it a humanitarian act, but according to scholar Robtel Neajai Pailey, such an agreement should have been approved by the legislature under the Constitution.

In Liberia, student leaders, civil society, lawmakers and ordinary people are questioning the secrecy and the decision taken without consultation: how will housing, treatment, screening and jobs be arranged, and how long will support last? There is also the fear that public anger will finally burst on these very deportees.

The writers point out that Liberia's own record on protecting refugees is also one of unfinished promises. They conclude that in this deal neither the deportees nor Liberians were heard, and both live under the same long shadow left by slavery.
nazar: For India this is not a far-off story. In 2025 America sent Indian migrants back in handcuffs on military planes, and inside the country there have been repeated charges of Bengali-speaking Muslims being pushed towards Bangladesh without a proper hearing.

When human beings become coins for bargaining in diplomacy, the poor, the homeless and the voiceless are the first to be put at stake. Governments of the Global South should ask their own people before signing such deals in exchange for aid.
sawal: Are human beings now just bargaining coins in diplomacy?
ref: American Colonization Society
A body formed in 1816 that sent free African Americans to West Africa and settled them there. This settlement became the independent country of Liberia in 1847.
Third-country deportation
Sending a migrant not to their own country but to a third country with which they have no link. Human rights groups see it as a way of getting around asylum law.

h: Climate resilience built on debt: women are paying the flood bill
dek: Bangladesh is praised for learning to cope with the climate crisis, but Shahrina Akhter shows that poor women are paying the price through microfinance loans.
body: Rehana lives on a char in Kurigram. Her vegetable patch, two goats and the raised plinth of her home were washed away in the Brahmaputra flood. To stand up again and pay off old instalments, she took three loans one after another. Shahrina Akhter, a researcher at United International University in Dhaka, writes in The Daily Star that Rehana's story is not an exception but a common story in Bangladesh's villages.

Bangladesh is called a model of climate adaptation, but according to the writer, a large part of the cost of this resilience is being borne through loans by the poorest households, especially women. Citing a 2019 IIED study, she says village families spend about two billion dollars a year out of their own pockets on preparing for and recovering from disasters, far more than the government and donors spend.

Of the more than three crore 20 lakh microfinance borrowers, about 90 per cent are women. This system, built for small businesses, now works in flood areas as informal insurance at commercial interest. Only 13 per cent of women in landowning households have farmland in their names, so they have nothing to offer a bank as collateral. Under the pressure of instalments they eat less, sell jewellery or take their daughters out of school.

Climate finance is talked about in billions of dollars, but according to the writer, less than ten per cent of international funds reach the ground. Her suggestions are clear: as soon as a flood or cyclone is declared, borrowers should automatically get a pause on instalments and relief on interest; there should be cheap adaptation loans for women and insurance linked to rainfall or flood levels; and money should go straight to women's groups and local bodies.
She concludes that making poor women pay for climate damage through costly loans is not justice. Help should arrive not after the next flood, but before the next instalment.
nazar: The story is the same in the flood districts of Assam, Bihar and Odisha. Loans from self-help groups and microfinance companies are taken in women's names, and after every flood the pressure to repay falls on them first. Women from Dalit, Adivasi and landless families, who have no land in their names, are trapped deepest in this web.

India speaks loudly about compensation for losses in climate talks. The same force should be seen at home too: without automatic loan relief after disasters and land in women's names, climate justice is incomplete.
sawal: In whose name, after all, is the bill for the climate crisis being written?
ref: Char
Islands of sand and silt in the middle of big rivers like the Brahmaputra, which keep forming and vanishing with floods. Lakhs of poor families live on them.
Loss and damage
The arrangement in climate talks under which rich countries help poor countries make up for losses from climate disasters. Agreement on its fund was reached at COP27 in Egypt in 2022.

h: Pilibhit's voter list: Asiya became Sofia, Akhlaq became Akhil
dek: After the SIR, the names of thousands of voters were found changed while their ID card numbers stayed the same, and no one had filled in a form for the change.
body: In Pilibhit in Uttar Pradesh, the names of thousands of voters have changed on the list, while their EPIC number and serial number remain exactly the same. The Congress alleges that 13,150 names were changed in the Pilibhit Sadar seat, the names of 884 people who still live there were cut, and 2,600 names were added of people who do not even live in the area. The party's UP in-charge Rajendra Pal Gautam said in Lucknow on 21 October that these changes were made between July and September, that is, after the final SIR list was published on 10 April.

An investigation by The Reporters' Collective found the same pattern on the ground. In the ten booths checked, no voter had filled in a form to change their name, and the booth level officers themselves did not know any changes had been made. About ten per cent of the names in these booths were found changed, and according to the report these lists mostly have Muslim names. One card has a young man's photo, the name Ashish Raj, and the gender recorded as female. In August alone, the state's Chief Electoral Officer approved seven thousand corrections.

Congress spokesperson Supriya Shrinate alleges that the changes came in clusters, which raises suspicion of tampering through software. The party has demanded an inquiry and said it may go to court. The report does not include any response from the Election Commission. The BJP won this seat in 2022 by about seven thousand votes.
nazar: If a changed name means someone cannot vote even with an ID card in hand, this is a quieter way of cutting names. When Muslim voters in particular appear to be the target, the Commission's silence itself demands an answer. The burden of checking one's name should be on the Commission, not on the citizen.
sawal: Who changes someone's name without a form being filled?
ref: EPIC number
The permanent number of the voter ID card, which links a voter to the list. If the name changes and the number stays the same, it becomes hard to catch the error.
SIR
The Special Intensive Revision of the voter list, that is, a fresh door-to-door check. Its methods have met protest in several states.

h: Uttarakhand's madrasas: Friday holiday ends, now it is Sunday
dek: A new holiday calendar has been imposed on recognised madrasas, and Muslim groups fear the autonomy of minority institutions is shrinking.
body: The Uttarakhand government has ended the weekly Friday holiday in madrasas recognised as schools and brought in a Sunday holiday instead. This is part of a new framework for minority educational institutions. The state Madrasa Board has already been dissolved, and after a law passed in August 2025 amid opposition protest, institutions of the Muslim, Sikh, Jain, Buddhist and Parsi communities will now run under the rules of the education department and the Uttarakhand Minority Education Authority.

The board had 452 registered madrasas. Under the new system, 76 have so far been recognised as schools and 114 applications are pending. The Authority's chairman, Dr Surjeet Singh Gandhi, says everyone will have to follow the department's holiday calendar, but Friday prayers will not be disrupted because government schools run until one in the afternoon. Chief Minister Pushkar Singh Dhami cited the Uniform Civil Code and spoke of one system for all. According to the minority welfare secretary, 250 unregistered madrasas were sealed in the first phase.

Muslim groups fear this will weaken the constitutional right to run their own institutions and practise their religion. The Congress questioned the government's priorities. Assam took such a step in 2016, while in Uttar Pradesh it was discussed in 2022 but the decision was not carried out.
nazar: A day off may seem a small thing, but when one community's custom is changed in the name of one rule for all, the message is not of equality but of dominance. Article 30 gives minorities the right to run their own educational institutions, and this right should show not only on paper but also in everyday arrangements.
sawal: Does equality mean making everyone the same?
ref: Article 30
This article of the Constitution gives religious and linguistic minorities the right to set up and run educational institutions of their choice.

h: Senator Blumenthal's 'India a failed country' video turns out to be a deepfake
dek: In the real footage the American senator was warning about purchases of Russian oil, not calling India a failed country.
body: A 19-second video spread on social media in which American Senator Richard Blumenthal appears to say that India's economy is collapsing and its army cannot win any war. It was linked to a bill imposing tariffs on countries that buy Russian energy and passed off as a real press conference. It was posted on X from one handle on 19 October and kept spreading.

BOOM's check found the real footage in an Economic Times report. In it Blumenthal is warning India and China not to buy oil and gas from Russia. He said this after the passage in the US House of Representatives of the bill that allows tariffs of up to a hundred per cent on countries buying Russian energy. There is nothing in it calling India a failed country.

In the viral clip the voice and lip movements do not match, and the jaw movement also looks unnatural, which is a common sign of a deepfake. A tool that detects fake voices also flagged it as made with AI. BOOM's finding is clear: the video has been tampered with.
nazar: Deepfakes are no longer just a tool for smearing opponents; they have also become a way to stir up a sense of national insult. In such times, pausing before forwarding every sensational clip is a civic duty, whichever side it seems to favour.
sawal: When did you last check a clip before sending it on?
ref: Deepfake
A video or audio made with the help of AI that shows a real person saying or doing something they never did.

h: Pakistan's journalist safety laws: strong on paper, weak on the ground
dek: A Freedom Network report says journalists cannot even reach the commissions set up under two 2022 laws.
body: In 2022 Pakistan made two laws, one federal and one for Sindh province, to stop the pattern of crimes against journalists and media workers going unpunished. Commissions were set up under both. A new report by Freedom Network, an Islamabad media watchdog, says these laws will stay on paper until the commissions get more powers, an easier complaint system and timely means of protection.

In a survey of about forty journalists in Sindh, 65 per cent said they had faced work-related threats or interference since 2021. 70 per cent knew about the law, but 65 per cent did not know where the commission's office was or how to complain. More than half said their employers had told them nothing about safety, insurance or legal help. The report itself admits this is a small sample, not a picture of the whole province.

The chairman of the federal commission listed shortages of staff and budget. The chairman of the Sindh commission denied there was a lack of trust and said 44 media organisations did not even reply to his questions. The report recommends confidential complaints, immediate risk assessment, dedicated caseworkers and making spending and outcomes public.
nazar: India has no national law at all for the protection of journalists, even though in recent weeks journalists reporting in Delhi have been detained. The neighbour's experience shows that a law is only a first step; the real test is whose door a small-town reporter can knock on when threatened.
sawal: If threatened, who can a small-town journalist turn to?
ref: Freedom Network
An Islamabad media watchdog that publishes reports on attacks on journalists and press freedom in Pakistan.

h: Immersion in Bengal: Chief Minister says only Sanatanis will touch the Durga idol
dek: Suvendu Adhikari asked for the identities of those carrying the idols to be recorded and claimed there was nothing communal in it.
body: On Bijoya Dashami, 21 October, while reviewing immersion arrangements at Babughat in Kolkata, West Bengal Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari said only followers of Sanatan Dharma would take part in immersing the idols. He asked the police commissioner to record the names and identities of those carrying the idols, and added that there was nothing communal in this.

The Alt News report points out that this is Bengal's first Durga Puja under a BJP government, and the word Sanatani was used a lot in this year's preparations. On 17 October, at least 19 people were reported dead in a stampede at a puja pandal in Chorbagan. That pandal was inaugurated by the Chief Minister, and his nephew is said to be its chief patron.

The same day in Jadavpur, there was a drive to remove book stalls of Left parties and citizens' groups, which local people opposed by forming a human chain through the night. In September the Chief Minister had told puja committees that if the CPI(M) used the word Sharadotsav, it should not be given space for a stall.
nazar: Bengal's Durga Puja has always been a shared festival of the neighbourhood, in which artisans and workers of every faith have taken part. Recording the identities of those who carry the idols is putting a guard on that sharing, and calling it not communal does not change what it means.
sawal: Why should anyone's identity be recorded to take part in a festival?
ref: Bijoya Dashami
The last day of Durga Puja, when idols are immersed in the river in Bengal and people embrace one another.

h: Coimbatore: Dalit student taunted over caste takes his own life
dek: The family of 16-year-old Class 11 student Akilan alleges the humiliation at school did not stop even after they complained.
body: A. Akilan, a 16-year-old Dalit student of Class 11 in Peelamedu, Coimbatore, took his own life at home on 21 October. His family alleges that classmates at school kept taunting him about his caste and his food. Things got so bad that last month he left home and went to stay with a relative. His father brought him back and complained to the school; the taunts stopped for a few days, then started again.

The FIR alleges that the class teacher asked the children who ate beef, after which two classmates hurled caste slurs at Akilan and beat him. His mother Kausalya's complaint names both students, the class teacher and the headmaster. When Akilan returned to school after the puja holidays, he was taunted again at the morning assembly, and his mother, coming home in the afternoon, found him hanging.

Police have registered a case under the SC/ST Prevention of Atrocities Act and sections on abetment of suicide and causing hurt, and have said they will look into the school's role. The allegations are still under investigation and have not been proven.
nazar: Caste humiliation often begins inside the classroom while the adults responsible stay silent. When a school cannot save a child even after a complaint, the question is not just about two classmates but about the whole institution. A binding system for complaints of caste discrimination in schools can no longer be put off.
sawal: What did the school do for Akilan after the complaint?
ref: SC/ST Prevention of Atrocities Act
A 1989 law that treats caste insult, violence and discrimination against Dalits and Adivasis as special offences and sets strict punishments.

h: Mysuru Dasara: three Dalit ministers stopped, Chief Minister orders inquiry
dek: Police stopped the ministers on their way to the Nandidhwaja puja, and the opposition called it a caste insult.
body: On 22 October Karnataka Chief Minister D.K. Shivakumar ordered an inquiry into the incident on Tuesday at Mysuru Palace, where police stopped three Dalit ministers from going ahead during the Nandidhwaja puja. Chief Secretary Shalini Rajneesh has been asked to identify those responsible and submit a report. According to the Chief Minister, the officers acted arbitrarily, and he stepped in at once to have the ministers called inside.

A video shows a police officer stopping P.M. Narendraswamy, K.S. Basavanthappa and Shivaraj Tangadagi as they were moving towards the puja site behind the Chief Minister. Muzrai (temple affairs) Minister Basavanthappa said he had not been told of any protocol restriction and that action should be taken against the officers responsible. The opposition BJP and JD(S) alleged that the ministers were insulted because of their caste.

Deputy Chief Minister G. Parameshwara played the matter down and advised against adding a caste angle to it. He asked why they were repeatedly being called Dalit ministers when the caste of other ministers is not mentioned. He accepted that there may have been a lapse, but said a small lapse should not be turned into a big controversy.
nazar: When even a minister's post cannot save someone from being stopped at the door of a ritual, one can imagine the situation of a Dalit in a village. Whatever the intent of the person who stopped them, the inquiry should make clear whom protocol is made for and on whom it is strictly applied.
sawal: On whom does a protocol lapse fall, and why?
ref: Nandidhwaja puja
A ritual held in the palace grounds on the last day of Mysuru Dasara before the Jamboo Savari (elephant procession), in which Nandi's flag is worshipped and the Chief Minister takes part.

h: Himachal High Court questions forest roads and Solan's tall buildings
dek: 55 roads and 16 helipads built without approval in Seraj came before the court, and it sought answers on construction above six storeys in Solan-Barog.
body: The Himachal Pradesh High Court has repeated that until further orders, no road may be built in forest areas and none may be tarred. According to Down To Earth's court digest, the amicus curiae's list records 55 roads in the Nachan forest division of the Seraj assembly constituency that were built in violation of the Forest Conservation Act, 1980, and in most cases the required proposals were not even sent.

The documents also showed 16 helipads in Seraj. The court voiced concern about the impact on wildlife and large-scale felling of green trees, and said an environmental impact assessment was needed. The court also questioned the legal basis of roads approved after August under the Forest Rights Act. The next hearing is on 2 December.

In a second case, the court sought the state's response on multi-storey buildings in Solan-Barog. A check of 21 projects found construction above six storeys in eight, while the height limit in hill areas is 25 metres. In the Barog patwar circle, 187 permissions were given to non-farmers to buy land or build, and 801 in Shimla district over the last ten years.
nazar: In the last few years Himachal has suffered cloudbursts, landslides and sinking buildings. If roads without approval keep being built in forests and tall buildings on the hills, the price is paid first by villages whose livelihoods rest on land and forest. If approvals were handed out under cover of the Forest Rights Act, that would go against the spirit of that law.
sawal: How many more roads and storeys can the mountains bear?
ref: Forest Conservation Act, 1980
Under this law, approval from the central government is needed before forest land is put to any other use.
Section 118
This section of Himachal's land law stops non-farmers from buying land in the state without special permission from the government.

h: Forest produce: women gather it, the middleman earns
dek: Families who gather mahua, tendu leaves and honey do not get even a fifth of the market price, though women carry most of the burden of this work.
body: Every year from February to May, Mamta Tigga of a village in Jharkhand's Gumla district gathers mahua flowers, gethi tubers and tendu leaves from the forest. Her husband is a driver, and when money runs short at home, this produce is their support. Usually she would collect four to five quintals of mahua in March and April, but this time, because of heavy rain, she barely got 25 kilos.

The report rests on a review published in 2026, written by Arkajyoti Dutta and Preyoshi Chakraborty of Vellore Institute of Technology. It examines forest produce in Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh and the Sundarbans. Dutta says government policy treats it as 'minor' produce, while the food, health, income and identity of crores of people are tied to it.

The sharpest figure is about how the price is shared. Less than 20 per cent of the price the customer pays reaches the gatherer. The value of tendu leaves rises about six times from forest to shop, but this gain does not reach the worker. According to the review, producer groups linked to e-TRIFED earn 28 to 35 per cent more than through the usual middlemen.

Women are the backbone of this work. Their share in collection and early processing is estimated at 60 to 80 per cent, and in Jharkhand they spend four to six hours a day on it, which is not even counted in household income. In Gumla's haats (weekly markets), too much produce arriving keeps weekly earnings stuck at 200 to 400 rupees. The Palakiya Foundation is taking leaf plates and mahua products made by women's groups to buyers in Ranchi.

According to the writer, there is an ecological danger too. Some Himalayan herbs, such as sarpagandha and kutki, have declined by 30 to 70 per cent in three decades, because the demand of the medicine industry is faster than the forest can recover. The review suggests that traditional methods, such as gathering only fallen mahua and rotating collection sites, be made part of forest management.
nazar: The Forest Rights Act recognised the gram sabha's (village assembly's) right over minor forest produce, but real power in the market still lies with the trader. Until Adivasi women's groups get direct prices, storage and buyers, their labour will keep becoming other people's profit.
The blows of the weather are deepening this inequality. One spell of rain almost wiped out Mamta's yearly earnings, and there is no insurance or compensation for it.
sawal: When will the woman who gathers mahua get the full price of her labour?
ref: Minor forest produce
Things other than timber that come from the forest, such as mahua, tendu leaves, honey and herbs. The Forest Rights Act 2006 recognises communities' rights over them.
TRIFED
A cooperative federation under the Ministry of Tribal Affairs set up to buy and sell Adivasi products. e-TRIFED is its online marketplace.

h: Sunita of Wardha: given the right to decide, she brought the farm back
dek: Amid rain-fed land, a husband lost to drink and wild animals, a woman farmer brought fields that had lain barren back under the plough.
body: Sunita Nehare of Pachod village in Maharashtra's Wardha district used to start her day at four in the morning. From six, for two hours, she worked on others' fields for a wage of 200 rupees, and then toiled on her own field till afternoon. The family had 12 acres of land, but because crops failed again and again on the sloping rain-fed land, only three and a half acres were being farmed. Her husband, in despair, had fallen into drinking.

After a big quarrel, Sunita was thinking of leaving home when her father-in-law handed the farming over to her. In 2018 she began with nine rows of cotton. The first crop was five quintals, the next eight, and later it reached 25 quintals from three and a half acres. Cotton yield per acre rose from one to one and a half quintals to more than seven quintals.

According to the writer, this change came from a climate adaptation project of the organisation Dharamitra, backed by NABARD. Field bunds, silt from ponds, raised beds, pigeon pea grown with cotton, crop rotation and homemade organic mixes were adopted, and Sunita says she no longer uses urea. Jowar, bajra, moong and sesame began to grow on land that had lain fallow for years. Water is still the biggest hurdle: drawing water from the farm pond costs about 12 thousand rupees of diesel every season, and in 2024 a well was dug under a government scheme.

In the last two or three years the crops have earned more than two lakh rupees. Sunita also works as a pashu sakhi, raises goats and poultry, gathers tendu leaves and is in the village savings group. Now other farmers in Pachod are also adopting her methods. Still, uncertain rain, hard labour and having no say over market prices remain her worries.
nazar: In this country women do most of the work on farms, but decisions on land, seed, water and money are rarely in their hands. Sunita's story shows that the real difference came from having the authority, not from some miracle technology.

We should also remember that this is one success story, not the rule. For lakhs of families in Vidarbha's rain-fed farming struggling with diesel, debt and falling prices, such stories will stay exceptions without irrigation and a guaranteed minimum support price.
sawal: When will a woman farmer's name appear on the land papers?
ref: Rain-fed farming
Farming that depends entirely on rain and has no irrigation such as a canal or tubewell. A large part of Vidarbha is like this.
Pashu sakhi
A trained village woman who handles vaccines, medicines and records for livestock. In Maharashtra this runs through livelihood missions such as UMED.

h: Climate's homeless: people no law protects
dek: Through Bangladesh, Colombia and the Pacific islands, this DW film shows that people uprooted by the weather are not even refugees in the eyes of the law.
body: This documentary by the German broadcaster DW is about a crisis that is less in the headlines and more in people's lives. The UN refugee agency UNHCR estimates that over the last ten years climate change has forced about 70 thousand people a day, on average, to leave their homes. The biggest price is being paid by poor countries, which did the least to cause this crisis.

The film's basic point is a legal gap. The 1951 Geneva Refugee Convention protects people fleeing persecution, but it does not treat a person uprooted by drought, flood or rising seas as entitled to asylum. There is still no universal legal framework to protect such people.

The first stop is Bangladesh. According to the film's description, about 24 lakh people there were displaced within their own country in 2024, mostly by natural disasters. Cyclones and storms, salt water creeping into mangroves and fields, and rivers swollen by melting Himalayan glaciers are together eating away coastal and riverside villages. For families made homeless by soil erosion and rising salt in the land, 'model villages' are being built there, where land is given along with a house.

The second stop is Colombia, where after a legal fight by lawyers, some people were recognised as victims of climate change for the first time. This ruling accepted that displacement comes not only from violence and armed conflict but also from the environment. In a country like Colombia, where decades of civil war uprooted lakhs, this is an important change.

The third stop is the island nations of the Pacific Ocean, some of whose very existence is threatened by rising sea levels. Policy there stresses regional solidarity, because people have a deep bond with their land and history. For them, leaving home is not just migration; it is the same as exile.
Instead of one hero's story, the film joins the experiences of three continents to raise a question: when a part of the earth is no longer fit to live in, who is responsible for its people?
nazar: India is not apart from this debate. The sinking islands of the Sundarbans, villages swallowed by the sea on the Odisha coast and sinking settlements in the Himalayas show that climate displacement has begun here too, but we have neither a count of it nor any policy for resettlement. Most of those uprooted are fishers, landless Dalits, Adivasis and small farmers, whose voices are already weak.

The politics of calling climate migrants from Bangladesh 'infiltrators' blurs this truth even more. People who cross the border after losing to the sea must be seen not as criminals but as victims of a shared crisis.
sawal: Why are people uprooted by climate not given refugee status?
ref: Geneva Refugee Convention
A 1951 international treaty that recognises as refugees people fleeing persecution on grounds of race, religion, nationality or political opinion. Climate displacement is not included.
Internal displacement
When people are forced to leave home but stay within their own country's borders. International refugee law does not apply to them.

h: Geni Cha's scissors: a memory of new clothes for Dussehra
dek: Vinay Saurabh's memoir in Sammukh uses a village tailor to recall a quiet togetherness that readymade clothes silently ended.
body: For Dussehra, poet Vinay Saurabh has written a memoir in Sammukh about Nonihat, the village of his childhood. In those days children got new clothes only twice a year, at Holi and at Dussehra, so waiting for the puja clothes was nothing less than a festival.

The market had four big cloth shops, and in front of them on the pavement the tailors sat under roofs of plastic and sacking. Most came from nearby Sadhudih and slept at the shop during the festival days. Among them Geni Cha (Uncle Geni) stood apart: a small rented shop, three machines and a cutting table. He only cut the cloth; other craftsmen did the stitching. The power was often out, so shopping happened in the light of a Petromax lamp.

The writer records with great honesty a child's restlessness, going round to the shop again and again with instructions about pocket flaps and black buttons, and also Geni Cha's calm, which each time gave the assurance that the clothes would be ready by Ashtami. Going out on the evening of Dashami in new clothes to spot a neelkanth was a ritual the whole village shared.

Then times changed. Young men from Sadhudih opened shops with signboards, the writer left for Bhagalpur to study, and readymade clothes took away the tailors' work. According to the writer, the shop of Geni Cha's son has been shut for months.

Geni Cha, who prayed five times a day and always wore a clean, ironed white kurta-pyjama, asked after the family at every meeting. The real message of the memoir is that such people quietly wove a social harmony whose worth is understood only after they are gone.
nazar: This memoir does not claim any big argument, yet two things stand out clearly in it: the festival of Dussehra passed through the hands of a Muslim craftsman, and the changing market left skilled hands without work.
At a time when efforts to divide festivals behind walls of religion are growing, remembering people like Geni Cha is itself an answer.
sawal: Where has the skill of village tailors gone now?
ref: Neelkanth
A bird with blue wings; seeing it on Vijayadashami is considered lucky in north India.
Petromax
A bright kerosene lantern, used in markets and at weddings when the power went out.

h: Viju Shah: the synthesizer wizard who lost out to consistency
dek: In Sammukh's 'Ilmi-Filmi' column, Aniruddha Sharma both praises the music of Kalyanji's son Viju Shah and lists its weaknesses.
body: Aniruddha Sharma, who writes on film music, has this time written about Viju Shah, who carried forward the legacy of Kalyanji-Anandji. His opening argument is that Kalyanji-Anandji's music stayed rooted in an Indian mood from the late fifties to the early nineties, even as names like R.D. Burman and Laxmikant-Pyarelal were rising.

According to the article, Viju showed talent at the age of four and was trained by his father. On a trip to Fiji he was introduced to the synthesizer, and at fourteen he did his first recording, for 'Don'. The writer believes this is where the duo's sound changed: the tune stayed Indian, but Western colours and a heavy orchestra began to be layered on it.

In 'Tridev' and 'Gupt', Rajiv Rai gave Viju a free hand. The writer says the contract had been signed earlier, so the credit went to Kalyanji-Anandji. He sees 'Gupt' as Viju's most ambitious work, which at first got a cold response.

The article is not limited to praise. Sharma charges that Rajiv Rai encouraged borrowing from English tunes, and he calls a song in 'Mohra' an almost complete copy of a composition by Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan. At the same time he calls the arrangement of 'Tip Tip Barsa Paani' unmatched.

His conclusion is that his father had advised simple tunes people could hum, but Viju got lost in technology and could not deliver good work consistently. Compared with his father's career, which lasted forty years, the son's journey stayed short.
nazar: This article is a reminder that in the film world credit often goes to the one with the name, not the one with the skill. Arrangers and musicians working inside the studio still live in this same obscurity.
The writer's frankness about copying matters, especially when the work of artists from across the border kept being used without credit.
sawal: Who should get the real credit in cinema?
ref: Arrangement
The work of setting a composer's tune in instruments, orchestra and layers of sound, which gives the song its full shape.
Synthesizer
An electronic instrument that makes all kinds of sounds from electrical signals; its use in Hindi film music grew in the eighties.

h: Shirish Dhobale's poetry: humility, longing and scattered manuscripts
dek: In Samalochan, Teji Grover reads Shirish Dhobale's new collection 'Anya Tattva' to understand a poet who keeps erasing his own footprints.
body: Poet and translator Teji Grover has written a long critical essay in Samalochan on Shirish Dhobale's new collection 'Anya Tattva' (Other Elements) (Setu Prakashan, 2026). She begins with an idea of the Sufi Mansur al-Hallaj, found in a book by Maurice Blanchot, about removing the 'I' that stands between the self and God. From this she asks where the poet stands between self-forgetting and madness.

In Grover's reading, Dhobale's journey is towards humility and longing. What is interesting is that the poet himself rejects the idea of a humble poet and sees poetry as intervention, yet the critic finds humility in his lines.

A moving part of the essay is about Dhobale's indifference to his own manuscripts. According to the writer, he sometimes forgets his own poems and asks readers to give them back. His long story 'Maharaas', about four women waiting to meet Krishna, has been lost, and the poet remembers only its outline.

The review reads both exploitation and tenderness in his poems on the earth and the Kshipra river, and links the poet to references such as Nietzsche, Akhmatova and Wallace Stevens. It sees his movement between the registers of Sanskrit, Hindi, Urdu, Marathi and Persian as his strength.
But this is not only praise. Grover says that in some poems an excess of words smothers the rhythm. In her view, Dhobale's ideal reader is one who lends a hand in completing the poem.
nazar: In a fast-moving literary scene shaped by social media, this review argues for slow, responsible reading. Criticism that freely lists weaknesses along with praise is becoming rare.
Poetry that moves between many languages stands against the single-language nationalism that wants to cut Hindi off from Urdu and Persian.
sawal: Is it the reader's job to complete a poem?
ref: Mansur al-Hallaj
A tenth-century Persian Sufi saint who was put to death in Baghdad for saying 'Ana al-Haqq' (I am the Truth).
Maurice Blanchot
A twentieth-century French writer and literary thinker, whose book 'Friendship' is a collection of essays on friendship and writing.

h: Fish without water: one story, a reckoning of many silences
dek: Govind Nishad's story in Samalochan looks at a rickshaw puller, a dying father and caste violence with the same restless eye.
body: Samalochan has published 'Bina Paani ki Machhliyan' (Fish Without Water), a story by Govind Nishad, a young writer and research scholar from Azamgarh. Since it is a story, we describe here not its text but its structure and concerns; the full story can be read at the original link.

The narrator is a young man who has come from the village to the city to study. In the scorching heat of Jeth (early summer) he crosses the Ganga on foot, and on the way an old rickshaw puller asks him not for money but for flour. Battery rickshaws have taken away his passengers, he is left out of a government scheme because he has no bank account, and his sons are lost in addiction. This meeting pushes the narrator into memories of his own father.

In the middle, the story opens a dreamlike layer. Buying fish on the bank of the Tons river, the narrator learns he has been sitting on the spot of a funeral pyre, and in his imagination a Nishad girl appears who was killed by her own people for loving a Dalit boy. The girl holds his silence, too, as part of the violence.

The last part is about the illness of his father Sadhu, who refused to go to hospital, and whose kidneys were ruined by painkillers. When the narrator returns with his fellowship money, the rickshaw puller too is nowhere to be found.

The metaphor of the title runs through the whole story: people from whom the ground to live on has been taken. The story offers no easy answer, and in the comments on the magazine, opinion is also divided about its pace.
nazar: Rickshaw pullers left behind by changing technology, the poor left out of welfare schemes, and the sword of caste over love: this story puts together questions that the news splits into separate boxes.
For a writer from the Nishad community to question violence within his own community, in his own voice, takes courage. Such voices deserve a place at the centre of literature.
sawal: Is staying silent also a way of taking part in violence?
ref: Nishad
A traditional fishing and boating community living along rivers, found in large numbers in Uttar Pradesh and Bihar.
Tons river
A river in eastern Uttar Pradesh that flows through Azamgarh and Mau.

h: The journey of 'Champwa ki Kaliyan': from Bhojpuri longing to the Japanese shamisen
dek: On Hindwi's Bela, Ashutosh Kumar Pandey uses a Bhojpuri song to read the movement of girmitiya migration, Bidesiya and folk culture.
body: Ashutosh Kumar Pandey's essay is not about a book but about a song. The folk-fusion band Maati Baani has presented 'Champwa ki Kaliyan' (Buds of the Champa) with the shamisen, a three-stringed Japanese instrument, Japanese artist Sayo Komada and Dhobiya dancers from Ghazipur. The song has a woman pining for her husband who has gone abroad, and the flower is the messenger of her memory.

The writer links this song to the long history of migration. In the nineteenth century, under the girmit (indenture) system, workers from Bihar and eastern Uttar Pradesh were taken to Mauritius, Suriname, Guyana, Trinidad and Fiji, and they carried their songs and customs with them, whose meanings changed on new soil.

In this tradition he places Mahendar Misir's Purbi songs and Bhikhari Thakur's Bidesiya, where migration becomes a story of poverty, a woman's insecurity and a breaking family. For the village, abroad was not only across the sea; it was also Calcutta.

The most interesting point of the essay is the reversal of direction: earlier the worker went abroad and home waited; now the song itself is travelling. According to the writer, real fusion happens when traditions listen to each other, not just when two instruments are played together. He also compares it with Caribbean chutney music.

The writer warns against treating Dhobiya dance as decoration, because it holds the memory of labour and community. He concludes that globalisation need not erase folk culture; culture can leave the village and also come back in a changed form.
nazar: Migration from Bhojpuri regions has still not stopped; in place of girmit there are now Surat, Ludhiana and the Gulf countries. So talking about the Bidesiya tradition is also talking about today's migrant worker.
Dances like Dhobiya are the art of working castes. Instead of making them an 'exotic' backdrop, their artists should get credit and pay.
sawal: Do folk songs stay our own even after they go abroad?
ref: Girmitiya
A word formed from the English 'agreement'; Indian workers sent to the colonies on contract in the nineteenth century.
Bidesiya
Bhikhari Thakur's folk theatre style and play, centred on the pain of a husband gone abroad and the wife left behind.

h: Through Tarantino: from Hollywood to the cinema halls of Allahabad
dek: In Hindwi's 'Unframed' column, Dinesh Shrinet uses Quentin Tarantino's films to return to the cinema halls and film memories of his small towns.
body: Dinesh Shrinet's essay moves between film criticism and memoir. When the season changes, he watches Quentin Tarantino's films again and finds that their roots lie in B-grade Hollywood, independent cinema and the Hong Kong martial arts films of the seventies.

Then he goes back to the cinema halls of Allahabad and Gorakhpur where he spent his childhood and teens. Drawing on Khalid Jawed's story 'Tafreeh ki Ek Dopahar' (An Afternoon of Leisure), he says the darkness of a cinema hall gives a short relief from the outside world, and the loneliness there does not become a burden.

According to the writer, Tarantino is born not of film school but of watching cinema. His style comes less from life and more from films. The death of Hitler in 'Inglourious Basterds' and the rewritten history of the Manson murders in 'Once Upon a Time in Hollywood' are examples of this.

The most interesting part of the essay is linking these references to India: Elvis Presley's mark on Shammi Kapoor, Kathmandu's hippie Freak Street in 'Hare Rama Hare Krishna', the Bruce Lee craze after 'Enter the Dragon', and Mithun's 'Wanted', whose poster called it India's first Western thriller. 'Mackenna's Gold', seen in Allahabad, formed the writer's first picture of America.
His conclusion is that Tarantino does not just revive old cinema; he sparks curiosity. The power of popular culture lies in the hints that lead the viewer towards a bigger world.
nazar: Single-screen cinema halls in small towns are closing fast, and a multiplex ticket is beyond the reach of working and farming families. This essay remembers that shared darkness where the rickshaw puller and the student watched the same screen.
Cheap cinema was not just entertainment; for small towns it was also a window to the world.
sawal: After the single screens, where will small towns watch films?
ref: Quentin Tarantino
An American filmmaker known for films like 'Pulp Fiction' and 'Kill Bill', whose films are full of references to old cinema.
B-grade films
Popular films made on low budgets, often shown alongside the main feature, which later became cult films.
